title: Food-tax relief can fail to reach poorer households when informality and market segmentation block price pass-through
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11453, Who Benefits from Food Tax Exemptions in Lower-Income Settings? Evidence on Pass-Through and Incidence
geography: Papua New Guinea; selected food items, formal supermarkets and informal stores across central urban and rural markets, with administrative data and a nationally representative household phone panel

observations.period: 2026 paper; unanticipated consumption-tax removal and price pass-through

denominator.unit: Papua New Guinea food-tax reform and multi-source price-incidence study

formal_urban_pass_through.value: complete pass-through in formal supermarkets in central urban districts

informal_rural_pass_through.value: no pass-through in informal stores or rural areas where poorer households mainly shop

data_stack.value: administrative data, supermarket price census, web-scraped online prices, and a nationally representative household phone survey panel

mechanism.value: competition, informality, and market segmentation determine whether tax policy becomes a lower shelf price

observations.method: Difference-in-differences analysis triangulated with administrative data, supermarket price observations, web-scraped prices, and a nationally representative household phone-survey panel.
observations.uncertainty: The pass-through estimates are specific to the selected PNG tax reform, products, markets, price measures, and time period; they do not establish identical incidence for every food tax or country.
observations.subgroup: Poorer rural households, informal-store shoppers, formal urban consumers, retailers, wholesalers, producers, and firms facing different degrees of competition and tax compliance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Observed price differences may reflect product composition, supply chains, quality, timing, or measurement coverage in addition to tax pass-through and market power.

observations.period: 2026 paper; fiscal-benefit incidence by household and market actors

denominator.unit: foregone-revenue incidence distribution across Papua New Guinea household quintiles and stores/wholesalers

poorest_two_quintiles.unit: percent of foregone revenue accruing to the poorest two household quintiles

richest_two_quintiles.unit: share of foregone revenue accruing to the richest two household quintiles

stores_wholesalers.unit: share of foregone revenue captured by stores and wholesalers

distributional_pattern.value: the exemption was highly regressive in the studied lower-income setting

observations.method: Incidence analysis combining household expenditure patterns, observed price responses, and market-level pass-through evidence.
observations.uncertainty: The incidence shares depend on the study's product basket, household consumption patterns, market coverage, and modeling assumptions; they do not measure every indirect welfare or producer effect.
observations.subgroup: Poor and richer households, informal and formal consumers, stores, wholesalers, and supply-chain actors receiving or losing fiscal benefits.
observations.counterinterpretation: Universal food-tax relief can still have non-distributional aims such as simplicity or broad political acceptability; regressive incidence does not mean every poor household receives no benefit.

observations.period: 2026 paper; policy comparison and expert expectations

denominator.unit: experts participating in the study's prediction survey

prediction_gap.value: the degree of regressivity and pass-through variation was not anticipated by the participating experts

cash_transfer_comparison.value: universal cash transfers would generate roughly two and a half times as much quintile-weighted value per fiscal dollar as the tax exemption under the study's static marginal-value-of-public-funds comparison

structural_explanation.value: high informality, market segmentation, and positive income elasticity of demand for basic food help make tax exemptions regressive

political_route.value: visible tax relief can be politically attractive while its realized incidence remains difficult for households and policymakers to observe

observations.method: Expert prediction survey and static marginal-value-of-public-funds-style comparison of tax exemption versus universal cash transfers.
observations.uncertainty: The cash-transfer comparison is static and depends on the assumed value weights, delivery capacity, targeting, and fiscal context; it is not a full general-equilibrium welfare evaluation.
observations.subgroup: Policy experts, households facing food prices, tax administrators, retailers, transfer systems, and political actors choosing visible cost-of-living relief.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cash transfers may be difficult to deliver reliably where registries, payment systems, or trust are weak; tax relief may be chosen because it is faster or more feasible despite lower distributional efficiency.

related_sources.claim: Abstract and bibliographic record for World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11453.
World Bank reproducibility package for the PNG food-tax pass-through and incidence study.
Institute for Fiscal Studies working-paper version of the study.

boundary: This record adds a policy-to-price pass-through and incidence route linking tax exemptions, formal and informal markets, rural-urban segmentation, competition, stores and wholesalers, household quintiles, expert prediction, cash-transfer comparison, and consumer cost-of-living politics. It is not a universal tax-incidence law, a full welfare or general-equilibrium model, or evidence that cash transfers are always administratively feasible or politically acceptable.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank working-paper PDF, abstract, reproducibility package, and IFS version were reviewed for the PNG tax reform, difference-in-differences design, price-data stack, formal/informal and urban/rural pass-through, quintile incidence, 237-expert prediction survey, cash-transfer comparison, and market-segmentation mechanism.
